title: AI transformation and the enterprise value gap
evaluation_goal: Assess whether a model can turn five source-separated evidence cards and three user-authored thoughts into a useful, accurate and original German LinkedIn post.

evidence_requirements.requirement: Establish the central value gap: organizational AI use is widespread, while measured or reported enterprise-level value remains limited.
Explain that workflow redesign and operating practices are associated with value, while preserving the survey's self-report, correlation and maturity limitations.
Use the customer-support study to show a real task-level productivity gain and its strong heterogeneity across worker experience or skill.
Preserve the distinction between the suggestive knowledge-transfer mechanism and what the customer-support study cannot establish about jobs, wages or other work settings.
Explain the jagged frontier using both the large gains on inside-frontier tasks and the performance loss on the selected outside-frontier task.
Avoid overgeneralizing the jagged-frontier experiment by acknowledging its task, evaluation, incentive or model-generation boundaries.
Use the P&G experiment to distinguish AI-enabled individual performance from human-team performance without claiming that AI replaces teams generally.
Capture at least one additional P&G finding about time, cross-functional expertise or emotional experience with its appropriate boundary.
Use the multi-firm Copilot experiment to separate measured email-time savings from unmeasured productivity or quality.

Connect the absence of detected task or process restructuring in an individual rollout to the open need for team- and firm-level complementary innovation, without treating the null result as proof that transformation is impossible.

synthesis_expectations: Build one argument around the difference between local task gains and organization-level value rather than presenting five mini-summaries.
Relate evidence from at least three sources and more than one level of analysis: individual, task or team, and organization.
Use evidence selectively; full coverage does not require naming every publication or reproducing every number.
Integrate all three user thoughts as genuine components of the argument, not as an appended list or falsely attributed research findings.
End with a useful implication or question that follows from the evidence and the user's perspective.

known_material_errors.description: Claims that more than 80 percent of companies measured no ROI or no financial benefit; the McKinsey item is self-reported lack of tangible enterprise-level EBIT impact.
Presents workflow redesign or CEO oversight as experimentally proven causes of EBIT impact.
Generalizes the 14 or 34 percent customer-support result to all employees, companies or knowledge work.
Claims that the P&G experiment shows AI can replace human teams generally or across complete innovation workflows.
Reports the Copilot study as measuring higher productivity, output quality or business value; it measured application behavior and time use.
Omits or reverses the outside-frontier performance loss and presents AI assistance as uniformly beneficial.
Attributes one of the user's personal thoughts to a study or presents it as measured evidence.
Treats the absence of detected task restructuring during the individual rollout as proof that AI cannot transform organizations.

evidence_coverage.calculation: Sum each evidence requirement weight multiplied by its status multiplier; weights sum to 25.

personal_thought_integration.calculation: Award five points per faithfully and substantively integrated personal thought, multiplied by status.

anchors.20: All material claims are supported, attributed at the right level and calibrated to each study's design and limits.
anchors.15: Accurate overall with one limited imprecision or minor unsupported flourish.
anchors.8: At least one major scope, causal, numeric or attribution error, or several meaningful imprecisions.
anchors.0: Critical errors or pervasive unsupported claims make the post unreliable.

anchors.15: Evidence from multiple sources and levels is related to build one original argument; tensions and boundaries do real explanatory work.
anchors.11: A coherent argument uses multiple sources but leaves one important relationship implicit or slightly list-like.
anchors.6: Mostly a sequence of source summaries with weak cross-source reasoning.
anchors.0: No meaningful synthesis or a conclusion disconnected from the supplied evidence.

anchors.10: Clear thesis, strong progression and a useful implication that helps the intended reader think or act differently.
anchors.7: Sound and useful, but predictable, weakly prioritized or missing a sharp implication.
anchors.4: The thesis is vague, the progression is uneven or the takeaway is generic.
anchors.0: No discernible argument or reader value.

anchors.10: Natural, credible German professional voice with an effective opening, readable paragraphs and no hype or template-like filler.
anchors.7: Generally suitable with minor stiffness, jargon, repetition or performative LinkedIn phrasing.
anchors.4: Noticeably generic, inflated, awkward or formatted like a report rather than a post.
anchors.0: Unusable for the requested audience and format.

anchors.5: High information value per word, within 400–550 words, short readable paragraphs and all format constraints satisfied.
anchors.3: Within the hard limit but somewhat overlong, compressed, repetitive or outside the target range.
anchors.1: Substantial padding, poor selection or distracting formatting.
anchors.0: Over 600 words, not meaningfully a LinkedIn post or materially violates the required form.
